title: The media: in print
subtitle: editorial, supplement, circulation, prospectus
summary: Name the sections of a newspaper or magazine and choose the right word for every kind of printed material, from a pamphlet and a flyer to a prospectus and a manual.

lesson.heading: Reading the paper
lesson.text: A reader describes her habits: 'One thing I always read in the paper is the **obituaries** page; it's so interesting to read about other people's lives.' An **obituary** is a description of the life of someone who has just died. She also reads the **editorial** (or **leader**), the article that gives the newspaper editor's opinion.

examples.text: The **obituaries** page is the first thing I turn to.
The **editorial** helps me form my opinion on things.
Yesterday's **leader** was a fierce attack on the government.

lesson.note: An editorial is also called a leader or a leading article.

lesson.heading: Covering the news, and selling things
lesson.text: National papers **cover** all the important news - they deal with it. The noun is **coverage**. But if you just want to sell your car, the **classified ads** (or **classifieds**) in a local paper are the best place: pages of advertisements sorted into categories.

examples.text: The paper's **coverage** of the election was surprisingly thin.
Only two papers **covered** the trial in any detail.
I sold the old van through the **classified ads** in the local weekly.

lesson.heading: Supplements, features and agony columns
lesson.text: Sunday papers come with **supplements** - separate magazines included with the newspaper, with articles on travel, food and fashion. A **feature** is an article, or a set of articles, devoted to one particular topic. Magazines often run **agony columns**, sections that deal with readers' private emotional problems, answered by an **agony aunt**. This sort of article really increases a publication's **circulation**, the number of copies sold.

examples.text: Last week there was a fascinating **feature** on new technology in one of the **supplements**.
I just can't imagine writing to an **agony aunt** about my marriage.
The magazine's **circulation** has fallen by a third in five years.

lesson.heading: Types of printed material
rows: journal
a magazine containing articles about a particular academic subject; also a book in which you write what happened to you each day
newsletter
a regular report with information for people belonging to a particular group
pamphlet
a small book with a soft cover, dealing with a specific topic, often political
press release
an official written statement giving information to the public and the news media
leaflet
a single sheet, or folded sheets, of paper giving information about something
brochure
a small, thin book like a magazine, giving information, often about travel or a company
prospectus
a small, thin book giving information about a school, college, university or company
flyer
a single sheet giving information about an event or special offer, often handed out in the street
booklet
a small, thin book with a soft cover, often giving information about something
manual
a book of detailed instructions about how to use something

lesson.heading: These words in use
lesson.text: The differences are small but real: a **leaflet** is loose paper, a **booklet** is stapled into a little book, a **brochure** sells you something attractive, and a **prospectus** sells you an institution. A **flyer** is pushed into your hand in the street.

examples.text: Part of John's doctoral research was published in an international chemistry **journal**.
I kept a **journal** while I was working in Zambia.
Laura is in charge of producing a monthly **newsletter** for her tennis club.
The company is going to issue a **press release** about its takeover plans later today.
Before you choose a university, you should send away for some **prospectuses**.

lesson.heading: Words about how books and magazines are made
lesson.text: A book has a **spine** - the vertical edge that carries the title - a **blurb**, the short description on the back cover written to make you read it, a **foreword** before the main text begins, and an **index** at the end. A magazine has **issues**, you buy a **subscription** to it, and a **quarterly** comes out every three months. An **edition** is used for both.

examples.text: The **blurb** promised a thriller; the book was anything but.
I've taken out a year's **subscription** to a photography magazine.
The June **issue** sold out in two days.

lesson.heading: Three useful publishing expressions
lesson.text: A **ghost writer** writes a book on somebody else's behalf, and the famous person's name goes on the cover. **Desktop publishing** means designing a publication on a home computer. A **facsimile** is an exact reproduction of an original, in every detail. And **small print** refers to the details, rules and restrictions in a legal document, often printed in very small letters.

examples.text: Troy Sutton's autobiography was actually written by a **ghost writer**.
It makes sense to use **desktop publishing** for a sports club's newsletter.
This book is a **facsimile** of an original edition published in 1693.
Always read the **small print** on a guarantee before you sign.

lesson.text: Cover is the verb, coverage the noun: a paper covers a story, and we then discuss its coverage of it.

exercises.prompt: Match each part of a newspaper or magazine with what it contains.

pairs.right: the lives of people who have just died
a separate magazine free with the paper
an article devoted to one special theme

exercises.prompt: Sales are falling: the magazine's ___ is down to 40,000 copies a month.
exercises.explanation: Circulation is the number of copies a newspaper or magazine sells.

exercises.prompt: I was disappointed by the paper's ___ of the strike - only three short paragraphs.
exercises.explanation: A paper covers a subject; the noun for the way it does so is coverage.

exercises.prompt: I've decided to do my own car maintenance, so I've bought the ___ for my particular model.
exercises.explanation: A manual is a book of detailed instructions about how to use something.

exercises.prompt: Someone was giving out ___ in the town centre today about a festival on Saturday.
exercises.hint: (single sheets handed out in the street, plural)
exercises.explanation: A flyer is a single sheet about an event or special offer, often handed out in the street; leaflets works here too.

exercises.prompt: I love looking through holiday ___ and dreaming about flying off to exotic places.
exercises.hint: (thin magazine-like books from travel companies, plural)
exercises.explanation: A brochure is a small, thin book giving information, often about travel or a company.

exercises.prompt: I never read political ___ ; they're so boring.
exercises.hint: (short soft-cover books on one topic, plural)
exercises.explanation: A pamphlet is a small book with a soft cover dealing with a specific topic, often political.

exercises.prompt: I wish I'd kept a ___ when I first started teaching.
exercises.hint: (a book you write your days in)
exercises.explanation: A journal can be an academic magazine or, as here, a book in which you write what happened to you each day.

exercises.prompt: The Central Bank has issued a ___ announcing some changes in personnel.
exercises.hint: (two words: official statement to the media)
exercises.explanation: An organisation issues a press release when it wants to give official information to the public.

exercises.prompt: I've read the ___ and I like that university; I think I'll apply.
exercises.explanation: A prospectus gives information about a school, college, university or company.

exercises.prompt: 'There's a new autobiography of the footballer Troy Sutton, but it was written by a ghost writer.' What does ghost writer mean?
options: someone who wrote it on Sutton's behalf
someone who did not have Sutton's permission
Sutton wrote it but used a different name
someone who edited Sutton's first draft
exercises.explanation: A ghost writer writes a book for someone else, whose name appears on the cover.

exercises.prompt: 'This book is a facsimile of an original edition published in 1693.' What is a facsimile?
options: an exact reproduction in every detail
a copy made on a fax machine
exercises.explanation: A facsimile reproduces the original exactly, down to the smallest detail.

exercises.prompt: Is each word normally used about books or about magazines?
